title: Cutting drink- and drug-driving: limits, testing and enforcement
label: 11 November 2026 · Road Safety Strategy evidence session
summary: Witnesses from policing, medicine, public health, academia and industry gave evidence on whether UK drink-driving limits should fall, how drug-driving should be detected and punished, and what enforcement and public-information changes are needed. They broadly support lowering alcohol limits and improving testing and prosecution, but disagree on whether saliva (oral fluid) testing can replace blood tests for legal thresholds. They urged better coordination, faster evidence chains from roadside stop to court, stronger sanctions where justified, wider use of treatment and technology such as alcolocks, and a major public communications push to change social norms.

chapters.title: Should the alcohol limit fall?
chapters.takeaway: Most witnesses urged lowering the legal alcohol limit, with many arguing for 0.02 for everyone and some supporting special rules for new and commercial drivers.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Scotland lowered the limit to 0.05. Should England and Wales follow?

turns.speaker: Dr Thomas Dolphin
turns.text: Yes. Scotland’s lower limit has been followed by fewer alcohol-related crashes over time. I favour 0.02 for new drivers because they need more concentration and are more easily impaired.

turns.speaker: Dr Richard Piper
turns.text: We want 0.02 for everyone now. Anything less leaves mixed messaging: campaigns say 'don't drink and drive' while the law still allows some drinking. Most of Europe is heading to 0.02 and the evidence shows much lower crash risk at that level.

turns.speaker: Ean Lewin
turns.text: In workplaces we see people misunderstand limits. Many would prefer a clear zero message. Breathalyser devices can be calibrated to lower levels, so it's technically possible.

turns.speaker: Chief Constable Jo Shiner
turns.text: Policing supports reduction. But deciding the exact level is for evidence and government, not for police. Our focus is on protecting victims and removing risky drivers quickly.

turns.speaker: Professor Kim Wolff
turns.text: Young drivers (17–24) are the highest-risk group; they should have very low limits. We should gather more evidence on whether a universal 0.05 with a lower limit for novices, or a 0.02 universal limit, is best.

turns.speaker: Dr Thomas Dolphin
turns.text: Most people can't measure their blood alcohol. Dropping the limit to 0.02 would send the clear message that there is essentially no safe amount to drink before driving.

chapters.title: Drug driving: scale and testing
chapters.takeaway: Drug-driving offences are rising; witnesses called for better testing and faster routes from roadside stop to prosecution, but disagreed on whether saliva testing can legally replace blood tests for thresholds.

turns.speaker: Rebecca Smith
turns.text: Do the Government understand how big and varied drug driving is now?

turns.speaker: Professor Kim Wolff
turns.text: They have lots of data, and drug offences now outnumber drink-driving. Cannabis and cocaine are the most common. But data is fragmented and should be pulled together.

turns.speaker: Chief Constable Jo Shiner
turns.text: On the ground it feels like an epidemic. We arrest many people under the influence. We need better evidence, funding and the new National Roads Policing Coordination Centre to co-ordinate action.

turns.speaker: Ean Lewin
turns.text: Roadside screening often fails or produces delays. In Operation Limit examples, police made many roadside drug arrests but relatively few prosecutions. We need a faster, simpler process.

turns.speaker: Rebecca Smith
turns.text: Should police routinely take saliva samples at the roadside to speed things up?

turns.speaker: Ean Lewin
turns.text: Yes. Countries like Australia and France use saliva: it gives quick, reliable screening, labs can confirm fast and prosecutions follow within days in some places. It’s cheaper and keeps drivers off roads sooner.

turns.speaker: Professor Kim Wolff
turns.text: I disagree about replacing blood with saliva for legal thresholds. Oral fluid doesn't map reliably to blood concentration, so you can't interpret impairment or legal limits from saliva except for a zero-tolerance test.

turns.speaker: Chief Constable Jo Shiner
turns.text: Policing needs a simpler, faster proof test at the roadside and the power to take licences there and then—either temporary or immediate—so we remove risks quickly while respecting procedural justice.

turns.speaker: Dr Thomas Dolphin
turns.text: Keep clinical staff separate from police sample collection. Using NHS staff to collect evidence could damage trust in healthcare.

turns.speaker: Ean Lewin
turns.text: We asked the Home Office about adding more drugs like ketamine to roadside testing. If legislation provides thresholds and the tests are approved, saliva could solve much of the delay problem.

turns.speaker: Dr Arthur
turns.text: You said many positives don't reach prosecution. Can you expand on why cases drop out?

turns.speaker: Ean Lewin
turns.text: Delays—waiting for transport, a healthcare professional, blood draws, lab analysis and court slots—mean evidence weakens or consent issues arise. Some cases simply never make it to court.

turns.speaker: Jacob Collier
turns.text: Are you suggesting the French or Australian model could be copied here?

turns.speaker: Professor Kim Wolff
turns.text: Those systems work within different legal frameworks and often use zero-tolerance oral-fluid testing. Our thresholds are blood-based; changing to saliva would need legal and scientific work.

turns.speaker: Ean Lewin
turns.text: If the law sets roadside-acceptable levels and the tests are type-approved, saliva could give high success rates for prosecutions, as shown in other countries.

chapters.title: Delays from stop to court and prosecution gaps
chapters.takeaway: Police, industry and public-health witnesses highlighted long waits from arrest to prosecution, many cases dropping out, and recommended faster lab processing, clearer prosecution pathways and possibly traffic or fast-track courts.

turns.speaker: Dr Arthur
turns.text: Why does it take months or years for some cases to reach court?

turns.speaker: Ean Lewin
turns.text: Because after a roadside stop there are many slow steps: transport, medical staff, blood samples, lab backlog, CPS decisions and court scheduling. That saps deterrence.

turns.speaker: Chief Constable Jo Shiner
turns.text: Faster evidence and simpler procedures would let us suspend licences immediately in many clear cases, removing danger from the road while allowing proper contest in serious ones.

turns.speaker: Professor Kim Wolff
turns.text: Speed is good, but courts need reliable evidence tied to the time of driving. That's why blood testing remains central for proving legal concentration thresholds.

chapters.title: Governance, data and coordination
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses want stronger national coordination—through the new road policing centre, a minister-chaired road safety board and a collision investigation branch—and much better, consistent data collection across agencies.

turns.speaker: Alex Mayer
turns.text: Does the DfT support enforcement well and who coordinates across agencies?

turns.speaker: Chief Constable Jo Shiner
turns.text: Partnerships are stronger now. The National Roads Policing Coordination Centre, funded by DfT, is a useful pump-priming step. A minister-chaired national road safety board should set priorities and reduce postcode differences.

turns.speaker: Dr Richard Piper
turns.text: Data is patchy—some forces don't submit figures. DfT should require standardised reporting so policy impact can be measured and targeted.

turns.speaker: Professor Kim Wolff
turns.text: Existing groups and DVLA data could feed a joined-up approach. The Road Collision Investigation Branch could pull lessons together, as other transport sectors do.

turns.speaker: Ean Lewin
turns.text: Show the Treasury cross-department savings from prevention: fewer hospital admissions and long-term costs if enforcement and communications reduce offending.

chapters.title: Prevention, sanctions and public messaging
chapters.takeaway: All witnesses said tougher sanctions help if paired with more enforcement, treatment for dependent offenders, technology like alcolocks, and a major behaviour-change communications programme aimed especially at younger drivers.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: What stops people reoffending and changes social norms?

turns.speaker: Dr Richard Piper
turns.text: Mandatory education courses after conviction work and are common abroad; they should be required here and mostly paid by offenders. Alcolocks should be enabled by vehicle design rules so they can be fitted.

turns.speaker: Chief Constable Jo Shiner
turns.text: Harsher bans for the worst offenders, more use of technology and quicker licence suspensions will reduce risk. Police do the job but need procedural tools to act quickly.

turns.speaker: Professor Kim Wolff
turns.text: Persistent drug-driving offenders might need a high-risk scheme with medical assessment before relicensing, like some drink-driver schemes.

turns.speaker: Dr Thomas Dolphin
turns.text: Psychology-led messaging works—phrases like 'don't let your mate drink and drive' change behaviour more than blunt 'don't drink and drive' slogans.

turns.speaker: Ean Lewin
turns.text: Random or workplace testing reduces offending because people believe they'll be caught. Faster lab confirmation after roadside sampling restores deterrence.

turns.speaker: Dr Richard Piper
turns.text: Lowering limits without better enforcement and communications will have limited effect: law, enforcement and messaging must come together.

turns.speaker: Joe Morris
turns.text: Any final quick points?

turns.speaker: Chief Constable Jo Shiner
turns.text: Keep measures simple and proportionate so police can remove dangerous drivers quickly and reduce victims' suffering.

turns.speaker: Professor Kim Wolff
turns.text: Review laws for new substances like nitrous oxide and test which drugs can be reliably screened roadside.

turns.speaker: Dr Thomas Dolphin
turns.text: Invest in treatment and mandatory education for those with alcohol or drug problems—these are cost-effective prevention measures.

turns.speaker: Ean Lewin
turns.text: If saliva testing and faster labs were adopted and legally accepted, we could close the prosecution gap and restore deterrence.

turns.speaker: Dr Richard Piper
turns.text: Adopt a Vision Zero approach: set bold targets to eliminate road deaths and back them with joined-up policy, enforcement and public engagement.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you all. Please send any follow-up evidence you couldn't cover today.
